title: Family 'in the dark' after son's death
subtitle: The SIU press release into the shooting death of Byron Debassige raised more questions than answers, says Kimberly Murray, the executive director of the Aboriginal Legal Services.
article: The SIU press release into the shooting death of Byron Debassige raised more questions than answers, says Kimberly Murray, the executive director of the Aboriginal Legal Services.

"It was dark and the ground, slippery with ice, sloped away from the officers as they retreated backwards from Mr. Debassige," who was advancing on them with a knife, noted James Cornish, director of the Special Investigations Unit, in his ruling that cleared the officers of wrongdoing.

At around 8:15 p.m. on Feb. 16, police received a call from a Davisville store clerk. An intoxicated man waving a three-inch blade had swiped a pair of lemons. Officers tracked him to nearby Oriole Park. Witnesses reported seeing him stumbling around, singing "Bad Boys," the theme from the TV show COPS, and begging for change, minutes before the shots.
Debassige was hit four times in the chest and one bullet grazed his arm.

"It says he had a three-inch blade knife, but then they go on to say it was dark. So how did they see it was three inches?" Murray asked. "Or, it says it there was snow on the ground. Is that a reason? Now it's okay to shoot someone when it's icy out?"
These types of questions, says Barry Swadron, the family's lawyer, are not unique.

"The family is left in an impossible position and this isn't the first time that it's happened," he said. "There's a complete factual blackout where the family doesn't know where it stands. Even now, when the SIU has come out with their decision, the family is still in the dark."

Michel Vigneault, Byron's stepfather, was there through the good years, when the "free-spirited" Byron still played with toys, was the jokester of the family and joined the army cadets. Vigneault was there through the bad years, when Byron began getting in trouble - drugs and drinking, skipping class, car theft.
He was there when Byron was diagnosed with schizophrenia and he was there when Byron refused his medication, turned to the street and began a decade-long cycle of moving in and out of jail.
It's been six months since Debassige was gunned down by two Toronto police officers. Now, Vigneault is there for his wife.

After the shooting, Jennifene Debassige's already ailing health fast deteriorated. Not long after hearing the news she suffered a heart attack. A few months ago, doctors realized her lungs were full of fluid. And just two weeks ago, her kidneys started to fail.
"I'm not looking for blood money or anything, I just want answers," she told the Star after the SIU made its decision.
